name: p3-0225-find-netns
title: Finding a container's network namespace from the node
spec: A flow. Left start 'You have a container or pod and need its namespace'. Two routes. Route A 'named namespace': 'ip netns add red creates /run/netns/red (a bind mount to the namespace)', 'ip netns list', 'ip netns exec red ip link', 'ip -n red link set lo up (-n is shorthand)', 'lsns -t net lists all network namespaces and their processes'. Route B 'anonymous namespace made by a container runtime (not under /run/netns)' (orange): step 1 'find the PID: docker inspect -f {{.State.Pid}}, crictl inspectp <pod-id> | jq .info.pid, or kubectl plus access to the node', step 2 'sudo nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr: runs host tools inside the namespace, so ip, ss and tcpdump work in a pod that ships without them', step 3 'ls -l /proc/<pid>/ns/net: compare inode numbers to see whether two processes share a namespace'. Right panel 'What a namespace holds': 'its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing tables, ARP and ND neighbour tables, netfilter rules, conntrack table, /proc/net, sockets, port numbers, and net.* sysctls'. Pod fact 'a Kubernetes pod shares one namespace among its containers; the pause container (sandbox) creates it, so containers in a pod talk over localhost; it also keeps the namespace alive across container restarts'. Bottom bar: 'Find the namespace before you run any network command, because host tools only see the stack of the host'.
alt: Two routes to a network namespace, a named one under /run/netns and an anonymous container one found by PID with nsenter, with what a namespace holds and the pause container.
cap: A named namespace is entered with ip netns exec, while a runtime-created one is entered by finding the container PID and using nsenter.

name: p3-0225-connectors
title: How a namespace reaches the network: veth, bridge, macvlan, ipvlan and SR-IOV
spec: A table of six devices with a mini sketch of each and its trade-off. 'veth pair: two linked virtual NICs, what goes in one end comes out the other, even across namespaces; a virtual patch cable with a plug in each room; one end becomes the container's eth0, the other stays on the host (ip link set X netns Y moves an end)'. 'bridge: software L2 switch joining veths, physical NICs and VXLAN devices'. 'macvlan: sub-interface of a parent NIC with its own MAC; packets go straight to the wire; the container appears as a separate host on the parent's LAN; host-to-container traffic on the same parent does not work unless the host has a macvlan sub-interface too' (orange). 'ipvlan: sub-interface sharing the parent's MAC with its own IP, L2 or L3 mode; good when switches limit MACs per port; L3 mode routes container IPs through the parent so there is no MAC explosion'. 'dummy, tun, tap, wireguard, vxlan, vrf: special devices for VPNs, overlays, VMs, routing isolation'. 'SR-IOV VF: hardware virtual function placed directly into a namespace'. Lower strip 'A physical NIC lives in exactly one namespace; a virtual interface can be moved'. Commands 'ip link add mv0 link eth0 type macvlan mode bridge; ip link set mv0 netns c1', 'ip link add ipv0 link eth0 type ipvlan mode l3; ip link set ipv0 netns c2'. Footer 'Other models: a routed veth has no bridge, one /32 route per container pointing at the host end with proxy ARP or a routing protocol (Calico); host networking skips the namespace; SR-IOV and DPDK bypass the kernel; macvlan and ipvlan may not work on cloud networks that filter MACs or IPs'. Bottom bar: 'Choose the model that matches what the workload needs: a NAT path, a LAN address, or a bypass'.
alt: A table of veth pair, bridge, macvlan, ipvlan, special devices and SR-IOV VF with what each does and its trade-off, including macvlan host isolation and ipvlan L3.
cap: A veth is a patch cable between namespaces, a bridge joins them, and macvlan, ipvlan or SR-IOV put a container directly on the parent's network.

name: p3-0225-container-paths
title: Three paths from a container: to a neighbour, to the Internet, and from outside to a published port
spec: Three horizontal lanes sharing a host with bridge br0 (10.10.0.1/24), containers c1 (10.10.0.11) and c2 (10.10.0.12), and an uplink NIC. Lane 1 'c1 to c2 on the same bridge': 'c1's own stack routes the packet because both share a subnet, ARP finds c2, the packet leaves c1's eth0 (veth peer), enters the host-side veth, the bridge learns the MAC and forwards the frame to c2's veth and eth0'; note 'br_netfilter and net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 let iptables see bridged traffic; Kubernetes requires it so kube-proxy rules apply'. Lane 2 'c1 to the Internet': 'default route points at the bridge IP 10.10.0.1; the packet enters the host IP stack, passes FORWARD then POSTROUTING masquerade, leaves through the NIC with the host's address; return traffic is un-NATed by conntrack and delivered back through the bridge; the outside world only talks to the host'; commands 'sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1', 'iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.10.0.0/24 ! -o br0 -j MASQUERADE', 'iptables -I FORWARD -i br0 -j ACCEPT', 'iptables -I FORWARD -o br0 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT'. Lane 3 'host:8080 to c1:80' (orange): 'iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.10.0.11:80', plus 'iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 127.0.0.1 --dport 8080 -j DNAT ... for local clients'. Footer 'DNS inside: mkdir /etc/netns/c1 and write nameserver 1.1.1.1 to /etc/netns/c1/resolv.conf'. Docker note 'almost literally what the default bridge network does: docker0, a veth per container, an IPAM address from a private pool, a default route via the bridge, masquerade, DNAT for published ports, a bind-mounted /etc/resolv.conf'. Bottom bar: 'A container is only a namespace plus a cable'.
alt: Three paths on a host with a bridge: container to container through the bridge, container to the Internet through FORWARD and masquerade, and a published port through DNAT.
cap: Container to container is L2 switching on the bridge, outbound traffic is forwarded and masqueraded, and a published port is DNAT to the container.

name: p3-0225-calico-routed
title: Bridge CNI versus routed CNI on one node
spec: Two panels. Panel 'Bridge-based CNI (bridge, Flannel host-gw)': pod A eth0 (a veth) to host-side vethXXX on bridge cni0 to pod B's veth to pod B; 'the node's pod CIDR such as 10.244.1.0/24 is local and the bridge IP is the gateway'. Panel 'Routed CNI (Calico)' (orange): no bridge; 'each pod gets a /32 route on the host, such as 10.244.1.5 dev caliXXXX scope link'; 'proxy ARP answers the pod's ARP request for its default gateway at 169.254.1.1'; path 'pod, veth, host routing, veth, pod'. Lab line 'pod default route via 169.254.1.1 dev eth0 onlink; proxy_arp on the host-side veths'. Bottom strip 'Cross-node: overlay (VXLAN, IPIP, Geneve) wraps the packet in an outer packet addressed to the other node: a route such as 10.244.2.0/24 via flannel.1, tunl0 or vxlan.calico, encapsulated in UDP or IP-in-IP; costs: MTU, CPU, pod IPs the fabric cannot see. Routed: node 1 holds 10.244.2.0/24 via <node2 IP> (static config, BIRD or the CNI daemon); needs L2 adjacency for host-gw, or a fabric learning pod prefixes over BGP; best performance, pod IPs visible in the fabric for firewalling and monitoring. Cloud-native: pod IPs come from the VPC subnet'. Debug commands 'ip route | grep 10.244', 'bridge fdb show dev flannel.1', 'tcpdump -ni eth0 udp port 8472 (Flannel, Cilium VXLAN) or 4789'. Bottom bar: 'Same pod to pod result, two different data paths'.
anchor: ### Same node, bridge-based CNI (e.g. bridge/Flannel host-gw)
alt: A bridge-based pod to pod path through a veth and cni0 compared with a Calico routed path using a /32 route per pod and proxy ARP at 169.254.1.1, plus overlay versus routed cross-node.
cap: A bridge CNI switches pod traffic on cni0, while Calico routes it with a /32 per pod and proxy ARP at 169.254.1.1 and no bridge.

name: p3-0225-docker-nat-bypass
title: Why a published Docker port ignores your firewall rule
spec: A packet path from the outside through the host firewall. Left 'Client on the office network or anywhere', arrow to 'Host NIC', then 'netfilter chains'. Show the order 'Docker's own NAT and FORWARD rules (DOCKER chain) are inserted ahead of the rules managed by ufw or firewalld' leading to 'container port 80' (orange arrow: 'published port 8080 answers from anywhere'). Beside it the firewall rule box 'ufw or firewalld rule that should block the port' shown skipped. Fixes box 'restrict a port with the DOCKER-USER chain', 'bind the port to a specific address (for example 127.0.0.1:8080:80)', 'if a published port must stay private on a shared host, restrict it in DOCKER-USER before you publish it'. Right panel 'Docker network modes': 'bridge: private subnet, veth per container, NAT outbound, -p publishes via DNAT; user-defined bridges add DNS-based name resolution and isolation', 'host: shares the host namespace, no isolation, no NAT, best performance, ports conflict with host: NCCL or HPC containers', 'none: only loopback', 'container:NAME: shares another container's namespace (how a Kubernetes pod works)', 'overlay: VXLAN across Docker hosts (Swarm)', 'macvlan or ipvlan: container on the physical network'. Model strip 'CNM: sandbox (the namespace config), endpoint (the attachment, typically a veth), network (a group of endpoints); local drivers bridge, host, none, macvlan, ipvlan; global driver overlay needs a key-value store'. Footer 'default subnet 172.17.0.0/16 may overlap corporate or VPN ranges: set default-address-pools in /etc/docker/daemon.json'. Inspect commands 'docker network ls; docker network inspect bridge; iptables -t nat -S DOCKER; bridge fdb show br docker0'. Bottom bar: 'Docker inserts its own rules ahead of the firewall's rules'.
alt: A client packet to a published Docker port passing Docker's NAT and FORWARD rules that sit ahead of ufw or firewalld, with the DOCKER-USER fix and the six Docker network modes.
cap: Docker's NAT and FORWARD rules sit ahead of ufw and firewalld rules, so restrict published ports with DOCKER-USER or a specific bind address.

name: p3-0225-cni-contract
title: The CNI contract: environment variables in, JSON in on stdin, JSON out
spec: Centre: a plugin binary box '/opt/cni/bin/bridge'. Inputs on the left. 'Environment variables: CNI_COMMAND (ADD, DEL, CHECK, VERSION), CNI_CONTAINERID, CNI_NETNS (the path of the namespace), CNI_IFNAME (such as eth0), CNI_ARGS, CNI_PATH' and 'Network config on stdin from /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf or *.conflist'. Output on the right 'JSON result: the IPs, routes and DNS'. Inside the box 'creates interfaces such as veth or macvlan and moves one end into the namespace', then 'calls an IPAM plugin for an address (host-local, dhcp, static, or a CNI-specific allocator)', then 'sets routes'. Below, the chained conflist as three boxes in order 'bridge: cni0, isGateway, ipMasq, mtu 1450, ipam host-local subnet 10.244.1.0/24' then 'portmap' then 'bandwidth'. Plugin families strip 'main plugins create interfaces: bridge, ptp, macvlan, ipvlan, host-device, vlan, loopback, dummy', 'IPAM: host-local, dhcp, static', 'meta: tuning (sysctls), portmap, bandwidth, firewall, sbr (source-based routing), vrf'. Test by hand 'CNI_COMMAND=ADD CNI_CONTAINERID=x CNI_NETNS=/run/netns/test CNI_IFNAME=eth0 CNI_PATH=/opt/cni/bin /opt/cni/bin/bridge < config.json, or cnitool; ADD first, then DEL to check cleanup'. Warning in orange 'stale /etc/cni/net.d files from an old CNI: the lexically first file wins; keep /opt/cni/bin and /etc/cni/net.d consistent across nodes'. Bottom bar: 'When a container starts, the runtime runs the plugin with ADD, and when it ends, with DEL'.
alt: A CNI plugin binary receiving CNI environment variables and JSON on stdin, calling IPAM, setting routes and returning JSON, with a chained bridge, portmap and bandwidth config and the plugin families.
cap: A CNI plugin takes CNI_COMMAND and related variables plus JSON on stdin, wires the interface, asks IPAM for an address and returns JSON.

name: p3-0225-cni-pick
title: Choosing a CNI: data path, policy and what each costs
spec: First strip 'Kubernetes network model: each pod gets its own IP; all pods communicate with all other pods without NAT, including across nodes; agents on a node such as kubelet reach every pod on that node; a pod sees its own IP the same way other pods see it; the CNI satisfies it with an overlay (VXLAN, Geneve, IPIP), routing (BGP or host routes), or cloud-native pod IPs from the VPC'. Table with columns 'CNI', 'Data path', 'Policy and notes'. Row 'Flannel': 'simple L3 overlay (VXLAN default, host-gw routed mode), Kubernetes API or etcd for allocations', 'minimal; no NetworkPolicy by itself'. Row 'Calico': 'routed (BGP via BIRD or Felix), optional IPIP or VXLAN overlay, eBPF dataplane; iptables and ipsets policy', 'strong NetworkPolicy; no overlay needed with BGP; integrates with fabric BGP'. Row 'Cilium': 'eBPF datapath replacing kube-proxy and iptables, identity-based policy L3 to L7, optional VXLAN or Geneve or native routing, Hubble observability, BGP control plane', 'high performance; requires modern kernels'. Row 'AWS VPC CNI, GKE native, Azure CNI': 'pod IPs are VPC or subnet addresses (ENIs, alias IPs)', 'no overlay; routable pod IPs; IP exhaustion and per-node ENI limits'. Row 'Antrea': 'Open vSwitch based, Geneve or VXLAN', 'policy; OVS offload options'. Row 'Multus' (orange): 'meta-plugin attaching multiple CNI interfaces to a pod with NetworkAttachmentDefinition CRDs', 'required for secondary RDMA and SR-IOV interfaces'. Row 'SR-IOV CNI plus device plugin, macvlan, ipvlan, host-device CNI': 'moves a VF or NIC into the pod's namespace', 'RDMA and GPUDirect data plane for AI'. Bottom bar: 'Ask what each plugin adds beyond basic connectivity, such as policy, encryption or secondary interfaces, and what it costs in return'.
alt: The four Kubernetes network model rules and a table comparing Flannel, Calico, Cilium, cloud CNIs, Antrea, Multus and SR-IOV CNI by data path and policy.
cap: Flannel is minimal, Calico and Cilium add strong policy, cloud CNIs use VPC addresses, and Multus attaches the secondary RDMA interfaces.

name: p3-0225-gpu-rails
title: A GPU pod's networks: primary eth0, secondary rails, and the NCCL interface variables
spec: Left: a pod box with two interface groups. 'eth0 from the primary CNI: control traffic, service access, logs, perhaps NCCL bootstrap; may be the overlay' and 'net1, net2 ... secondary interfaces: RDMA-capable NICs (ConnectX in RoCE or IB mode) for high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU and storage traffic'. Arrows from the secondary interfaces to 'Rails: rail0, rail1, ...'. Middle: how the secondary interface is attached as a chain 'NVIDIA Network Operator, Multus (NetworkAttachmentDefinition), SR-IOV device plugin with SR-IOV CNI (places VFs into the pod), host-device, macvlan or ipvlan CNI, RDMA shared device plugin (rdma/hca_shared_devices_a)'. Pod spec snippets 'annotation k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: rail0', 'resources: nvidia.com/gpu: 8, nvidia.com/rdma_shared_device_a: 1 or nvidia.com/sriov_net: 8', 'securityContext capabilities add IPC_LOCK: RDMA memory registration, so the pod can pin memory', 'NetworkAttachmentDefinition rail0: macvlan, master ens1f0, mode bridge, mtu 9000, ipam whereabouts range 10.100.0.0/24'. Right panel 'Tell NCCL which interface' (orange): 'NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME controls bootstrap and socket transport', 'NCCL_IB_HCA selects the RDMA devices', 'NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX selects the RoCE GIDs', 'example NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=net1 and NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0,mlx5_1', 'or run with hostNetwork'. Failure story 'the first interface NCCL sees may be the overlay; the job runs, but every collective crosses the overlay, and nothing logs an error'. Bottom bar: 'Make the fast path the default by naming the interfaces the library should use'.
anchor: ## 6. Networking for GPU and HPC pods
alt: A GPU pod with a primary eth0 overlay interface and secondary net1 rail interfaces attached by Multus and SR-IOV, with IPC_LOCK, the NetworkAttachmentDefinition and the NCCL interface variables.
cap: A GPU pod needs secondary RDMA interfaces attached through Multus and SR-IOV, and NCCL must be told to use them instead of the eth0 overlay.

name: p3-0225-gpu-pod-points
title: Ten things to decide for a GPU or HPC pod's network
spec: A numbered table with ten rows, each a decision and its rule. '1 Primary versus data plane: eth0 for control, secondary RDMA NICs for GPU and storage traffic'. '2 NCCL interface selection: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_IB_HCA, NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX set explicitly'. '3 Host networking: hostNetwork true with dnsPolicy ClusterFirstWithHostNet; simplest high-performance option; costs port conflicts, less isolation, no per-pod NetworkPolicy'. '4 Overlay costs: small packets, many connections and large flows suffer crossing a veth, a bridge and an overlay (CPU softirq and a smaller MTU); prefer native routing CNIs or eBPF host routing for TCP-heavy services; overlay MTU is underlay minus 50 for VXLAN; verify with ping -M do'. '5 Topology alignment: kubelet Topology Manager single-numa-node or best-effort with the CPU Manager and device plugins keeps GPU, NIC VF and CPUs on the same NUMA node or PCIe root; verify with nvidia-smi topo -m and ibdev2netdev'. '6 MTU consistency: pod MTU is node MTU minus encapsulation; secondary rails often 9000 and the CNI mtu must match the fabric'. '7 Isolation and policy: NetworkPolicy with default deny per namespace covers the primary network; secondary SR-IOV and macvlan interfaces bypass host policy: isolate with VLANs, VRFs or IB partitions at the switch' (orange). '8 IPAM: size the pod CIDR against nodes and pods per node; a /24 per node gives 254 pods; secondary networks may use whereabouts or static ranges, one per rail'. '9 Observability: Hubble or Cilium flow logs, Calico flow logs, kube-state and CNI metrics, ethtool -S for VFs, RDMA counters, nsenter into a pod's namespace'. '10 Upgrades: CNI changes can reset pod networks; stage them, drain nodes, canary clusters first; keep /opt/cni/bin and /etc/cni/net.d consistent'. Side note 'hostNetwork pods share the node's IP and port space and skip the CNI; node agents such as kube-proxy, the CNI daemon, node-exporter and the DCGM exporter run this way; check for port conflicts before scheduling'. Bottom bar: 'Decide the rails before you write the pod spec'.
anchor: ## 6. Networking for GPU and HPC pods
alt: A ten row table of GPU pod network decisions: primary versus data plane, NCCL interfaces, host networking, overlay costs, topology alignment, MTU, isolation, IPAM, observability and upgrades.
cap: Ten decisions shape a GPU pod's network, from rails and NCCL interfaces to NUMA alignment, MTU, policy bypass on secondary NICs and CNI upgrades.

name: p3-0225-numa-align
title: Keeping the GPU, its NIC and its CPUs on one NUMA node
spec: Two panels showing two CPU sockets 'NUMA node 0' and 'NUMA node 1' with a link between them. Panel 'Aligned': GPU, NIC VF or RDMA device, and the pod's CPUs all on NUMA node 0; transfers stay inside the node; fast. Panel 'Misaligned' (orange): pod CPUs on node 0 but the NIC on node 1; every transfer crosses the link between sockets and takes the slower road. Right: how to keep them together 'kubelet Topology Manager with the single-numa-node or best-effort policy, together with the CPU Manager and the device plugins'. 'Verify after the pod starts: nvidia-smi topo -m, ibdev2netdev'. Beside it a note 'same on the host: pin test CPUs to the NUMA node of the NIC'. Bottom bar: 'A scheduler can place CPUs on one node and the network card on the other, so check the placement after the pod starts'.
anchor: ## 6. Networking for GPU and HPC pods
alt: An aligned layout with the GPU, NIC and CPUs on one NUMA node versus a misaligned layout where transfers cross the socket link, with the Topology Manager policies that keep them together.
cap: The Topology Manager keeps the GPU, NIC and CPUs on one NUMA node so transfers avoid the slower link between sockets.

name: p3-0225-veth-peer
title: Which host veth belongs to this pod: pairing by ifindex
spec: A two-panel diagram. Left panel 'Inside the pod namespace': 'eth0 (the pod end of the veth pair)' with the command 'sudo nsenter -t <pid> -n ethtool -S eth0 | grep peer_ifindex' returning 'peer_ifindex: N'. Right panel 'On the host': a list of host interfaces 'lo', 'eth0 or the uplink', 'cni0 or the node's routing device', 'vethXXX (index N)', 'vethYYY', with the command 'ip -o link | grep ^N:' matching index N. Arrow between the two labelled 'same number: this host veth is the other end of the pod's eth0'. Use cases beneath: 'capture on the pod's veth from the host', 'find which bridge port or Calico caliXXXX route belongs to the pod'. Process flow top: 'crictl pods --name trainer-0', 'crictl inspectp <pod-id> | jq .info.pid', 'nsenter -t <pid> -n ip -br addr, ip route, ss -tulpn', 'kubectl debug -it trainer-0 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=pytorch' for an ephemeral debug container. Bottom bar: 'nsenter runs the tools of the host inside the namespace of the pod'.
alt: Pairing a pod's eth0 peer_ifindex from ethtool -S inside the namespace with the matching host veth in ip -o link, with the crictl and nsenter steps to get the PID.
cap: The peer_ifindex reported inside a pod matches the index of its veth on the host, which shows where to capture or look for routes.

name: p3-0225-hostnet-tradeoff
title: hostNetwork versus CNI for GPU jobs, and the mistakes that bite
spec: Two columns. Column 'hostNetwork: true with dnsPolicy ClusterFirstWithHostNet': 'shares the node's namespace, IP and port space; skips the CNI and uses host ports; DNS policy uses the host's DNS config', 'pros: simplest high-performance option, no overlay, node agents such as kube-proxy, CNI daemon, node-exporter, DCGM exporter and NCCL over sockets run this way', 'cons: port conflicts, less isolation, no per-pod NetworkPolicy', 'common in single-tenant clusters and MPI or Slurm-on-Kubernetes'. Column 'Pod network through the CNI': 'own namespace, own IP, pause container owns the namespace; kubelet writes /etc/resolv.conf to point at CoreDNS with search domains and ndots:5', 'pros: isolation, policy, per-pod IPs', 'cons: veth, bridge and overlay costs; smaller MTU'. Bottom list 'Eight mistakes' as two rows: 'lo not up inside a namespace', 'forgot ip_forward or masquerade', 'container subnets overlap with host or VPN ranges', 'bridged traffic invisible to iptables without br_netfilter settings', 'eth0 used inside GPU pods for NCCL, so traffic goes through the overlay' (orange), 'overlay MTU unreduced or jumbo frames only on some nodes', 'debugging with host-only tools instead of nsenter', 'macvlan containers expected to reach the host, or macvlan and ipvlan on clouds that filter MACs or IPs', 'NetworkPolicy assumed to cover SR-IOV or RDMA secondary interfaces', 'CNI config changed without draining nodes'. Bottom bar: 'Read the list as questions to ask before the first pod is scheduled'.
alt: A comparison of hostNetwork and CNI networking for pods, with pros and cons, and a list of common container networking mistakes.
cap: hostNetwork gives simple high performance at the cost of isolation and port conflicts, while CNI networking gives isolation and policy at an overlay cost.
